newsitem.title: UK: Four UK ex-Conservative MPs criticised on sleaze.
newsitem.headline: Four UK ex-Conservative MPs criticised on sleaze.

text.p: A British parliamentary report on Thursday attacked two former Conservative ministers for conduct "well below the standards expected of members of parliament" in accepting cash from a businessman for lobbying on his behalf.

The report from parliament's standards commissioner Sir Gordon Downey said Tim Smith received at least 18,000 pounds ($30,150) from Mohammed Al-Fayed while Neil Hamilton got an amount which was unknown but probably at least as great.

The long-awaited report also criticised two other former Conservative legislators for receiving money from parliamentary lobbyist Ian Greer and failing to register the payments in the register of MPs' interests. But it said allegations against six other former MPs could not be substantiated.

The report will now be considered by parliament's Standards and Privileges Committee. But because none of the MPs criticised retained their seats at the May 1 election, it will have severely limited powers to punish them. Allegations of sleaze cast a shadow over the Conservatives in the run-up to the May 1 election.
Cash-for-questions charges against Hamilton in particular created an impression among voters of a party grown too used to the trappings of power after 18 years in office.
The Labour Party even claimed that former prime minister John Major called the election early to prevent Downey's report from being published before the voters gave their verdict.
Public disquiet prompted Martin Bell, a former BBC war correspondent, to stand successfully against Hamilton in the election on an independent anti-sleaze platform.

Bell's candidacy led to the most memorable scene of the election, when he was unexpectedly confronted by Hamilton and his fiercely loyal wife Christine and challenged to say whether he was trying to ruin the former minister's political career.
The report said that in addition to receiving cash from Fayed, Hamilton had been entertained at his luxury Ritz Hotel in Paris.
"The hospitality Mr Hamilton received from Mr Al Fayed....was intended and accepted as part of his reward for lobbying. It was not, as it should have been, registered," the report said.
Downey also said that Hamilton "deliberately misled" the then Trade and Industry Secretary Michael Heseltine when he questioned him about the allegations against him.

"I don't accept Sir Gordon's finding. I don't accept that I took this money from Mr Fayed. Sir Gordon has not been able to identify when this money was paid, how much was paid, why it was paid or where the money went," Hamilton told Channel Four television news.
Hamilton has always strenuously denied accepting envelopes stuffed with cash in return for asking questions in parliament on behalf of the Egyptian-born businessman.
But he had admitted breaking House of Commons rules by inadvertently failing to declare hospitality at the Paris Ritz.
Smith resigned from his ministerial post when the allegations surfaced and did not contest the election.
The other former members criticised in the report are Sir Andrew Bowden and Sir Michael Grylls.
It said Bowden failed to declare an election donation from parliamentary lobbyist Ian Greer, and Grylls deliberately misled a parliamentary committee about payments by Greer. ($1=.5970 Pound)
